items.title: Venn diagrams — class relationships and region counts
items.body:
### Venn diagrams — class relationships and region counts

**The idea in one sentence**
A Venn diagram draws one circle for each group so you can either pick the picture that matches the words or read the numbers region by region.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Take a tiny class of 10 children: 6 like tea, 5 like coffee, 3 like both. How many like at least one drink? List it out. The 3 who like both are already counted inside the 6 tea-lovers and again inside the 5 coffee-lovers. If you just add 6 + 5 = 11 you have counted those 3 children twice. Remove that double-count once: 11 − 3 = 8 like at least one drink, and the remaining 10 − 8 = 2 like neither. Nothing was memorised — you simply refused to count the same child twice.

**Why remove the overlap only once?**
The 3 who like both sit in the lens where the two circles cross. Adding the two circle totals counts that lens twice, so you subtract it exactly one time to put the count right.

```
 Tea(6)        Coffee(5)
 [ 3 ]  ( 3 )  [ 2 ]
 only    both   only   -> 3 + 3 + 2 = 8
```

**What the symbols mean**
- n(A) means the number of things in group A.
- A union B means everything in A or B or both.
- A intersection B means the things in both A and B (the overlap).
- only A means in A but in no other group.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Two groups: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(both); people in neither = total − n(A or B). Three groups: at least one = (sum of the three singles) − (sum of the three pair-overlaps) + (all three). Reading regions: exactly one = the three only-slices added; exactly two = the three only-two slices added, and this does NOT include the all-three centre.

**Exam-level example**
Survey of 120: English 65, Hindi 45, Telugu 42; English and Hindi 20, Hindi and Telugu 25, English and Telugu 15, all three 8. At least one = 65 + 45 + 42 − 20 − 25 − 15 + 8 = 152 − 60 + 8 = 100. Check the slow way: start at 152, strip the double-counted pair readers (60); that strips the all-three readers one time too many, so add them back once (+8) to reach 100.

**Common traps**
- Adding the circle totals but forgetting to subtract the overlap, which over-counts.
- Treating exactly two as if it included the all-three centre.
- Mixing at least one (anyone in a circle) with exactly one (only the three single slices).

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(both) | add the two groups, remove the shared part once |
| exactly one = only A + only B + only C | add just the three outer slices |
| at least one = total − neither | everyone who is in some circle |
keyPoints: Subset (all A are B) is a small circle inside a big one; some-are is two overlapping circles; no-A-is-B is two separate circles.
Two coordinate classes under one genus (Table, Chair under Furniture) are two separate circles inside a larger circle.
Exactly one = the three only-slices added; exactly two excludes the all-three centre.
Two groups: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(both); neither = total − n(A or B).
At least one = total − the neither region.

items.title: Mirror and water images
items.body:
### Mirror and water images

**The idea in one sentence**
A mirror image flips a shape left-to-right and a water image flips it top-to-bottom, so a letter looks unchanged only when the half being swapped already matches its other half.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Write the word CODE and hold a small mirror along its right-hand edge. Copy what you see, reading from the mirror edge outwards: the letter nearest the mirror (E) now appears first, then D, then O, then C, giving E-D-O-C. Do not reach for a rule — just read the reflection from the mirror outwards and the reversal is obvious. Each single letter is also turned back-to-front, but the thing the exam tests is the ORDER, which is simply the word written backwards.

**Why does a mirror reverse the order but water keeps it?**
A side mirror swaps left and right, so the letter that was on the far right ends up nearest you and the sequence flips. Still water sits below the word and swaps up and down only; left-to-right is untouched, so letters keep their order but each turns upside down.

```
 actual clock 4:30  ->  mirror 7:30
 rule: subtract the time from 11:60
```

**What the symbols mean**
- vertical mirror means a mirror standing on its side (left or right), giving a left-right flip.
- water image means the reflection seen in water below, a top-bottom flip.
- 11:60 means 12:00 written so minutes subtract easily (60 minutes = 1 hour).

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Mirror of a word = its letters in reverse order. Capitals unchanged by a vertical mirror (left-right symmetry): A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y. Capitals unchanged by a water image (top-bottom symmetry): B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X. Mirror-clock time = 11:60 − actual time.

**Exam-level example**
A wall clock shows 8:20; find its mirror time. Work out 11:60 − 8:20: minutes 60 − 20 = 40, hours 11 − 8 = 3, giving 3:40. Check the slow way: at 8:20 the hour hand sits two-thirds of the way from 8 to 9, and its mirror lands two-thirds of the way from 3 to 4, which reads 3:40. Note that H, I, O, X carry both kinds of symmetry, so they look identical in a mirror AND in water.

**Common traps**
- Offering the mirror set of letters as the answer to a water-image question — the two sets are different.
- Reflecting the hour but forgetting to reflect the minutes in a clock problem.
- Using 12:00 instead of 11:60 and mishandling the minute borrow.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| CODE becomes EDOC | a mirror writes the word backwards |
| A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y | capitals unchanged in a side mirror |
| 11:60 − time | the clock's mirror time |
keyPoints: Mirror image is a left-right flip; a word's letter order reverses, so CODE becomes EDOC.
Capitals unchanged in a side mirror: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.
Water image is a top-bottom flip; capitals unchanged: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X.
Mirror-clock time = 11:60 − actual time (so 4:30 becomes 7:30).
H, I, O, X are unchanged in both the mirror and the water image.
items.mnemonic: Side mirror = write it backwards; water = flip top to bottom.

items.title: Painted cubes, cube stacks and dice
items.body:
### Painted cubes, cube stacks and dice

**The idea in one sentence**
A big painted cube cut into small cubes gives four kinds of small cube depending on how many painted faces show, and dice puzzles are solved by tracking which faces end up opposite one another.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Paint a cube red and slice it into a 3-by-3-by-3 block of 27 small cubes. Walk around it and sort the little cubes by hand. The 8 corner cubes each touch three outer faces, so they have 3 painted faces. The cubes in the middle of each edge (not corners) touch two outer faces, so 2 painted. The cube at the centre of each big face touches one outer face, so 1 painted. The single cube buried inside touches nothing, so 0 painted. Counting: corners 8, edge-middles 12, face-centres 6, hidden 1, and 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27, every cube accounted for.

**Why does the count split like that?**
Paint only reaches the outer surfaces. A corner meets three surfaces, an edge two, a face one, and the buried core none, so a small cube's position alone fixes how many painted faces it has.

```
 corner = 3 faces | edge = 2 | face-centre = 1 | core = 0
```

**What the symbols mean**
- n means how many small cubes lie along one edge, so the total is n times n times n.
- (n − 2) means the edge cubes that are left after dropping the two corners at the ends.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
For n small cubes per edge: three-face corners = 8 (always); two-face edges = 12 × (n − 2); one-face centres = 6 × (n − 2)²; zero-face core = (n − 2)³. The four counts add back to n × n × n. A cube itself has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. For a stepped stack, count each layer and add; a stack holds fewer cubes than its boxy outline.

**Exam-level example**
A cube is painted and cut into 125 equal cubes; how many show exactly one face? Here 125 = 5 × 5 × 5, so n = 5. One-face cubes = 6 × (5 − 2)² = 6 × 9 = 54. Check: corners 8, edges 12 × 3 = 36, faces 54, core 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, and 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125. Dice tip: with two views that share one face, the shared face stays put while the others turn around it, and two faces are opposite when they can never sit side by side.

**Common traps**
- Using 6 × (n − 2) instead of 6 × (n − 2)² for the one-face cubes.
- Calling 12 (the number of edges) the edge-cube count; it is 12 × (n − 2).
- Assuming a stepped stack fills its full bounding box.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| 8 corners | always three painted faces |
| 12(n − 2) | cubes along the edges, two painted |
| 6(n − 2)² | face-centre cubes, one painted |
| (n − 2)³ | hidden core, no paint |
keyPoints: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices; the 8 corner cubes always show 3 painted faces.
Painted-cube counts: 3-face = 8, 2-face = 12(n − 2), 1-face = 6(n − 2)², 0-face = (n − 2)³.
The four painted-face counts add back to n times n times n (n = cubes per edge).
Count a stack layer by layer; a stepped stack has fewer cubes than its bounding box.
Dice: keep the shared face fixed; opposite faces are the pair that never sit side by side.

items.title: Paper folding, dot placement, pattern grids and hidden figures
items.body:
### Paper folding, dot placement, pattern grids and hidden figures

**The idea in one sentence**
These four non-verbal types all reward one habit: track exactly what each fold, overlap, rule or outline does, step by step, instead of guessing the final picture.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Take a square sheet and fold it once; now 2 layers are stacked. Fold again; those 2 layers double to 4. Punch one hole through the stack, away from the creases, and unfold slowly. The first unfold shows the hole mirrored across the last crease (2 holes); the second unfold mirrors that pair across the first crease (4 holes). You counted 4 just by watching the layers: one hole for every layer the punch passed through.

**Why does each fold double the holes?**
A fold lays the paper on top of itself, so every existing layer becomes two. The single punch pierces all layers at once, and each pierced layer opens out into its own hole.

```
 0 folds: 1 layer   1 fold: 2   2 folds: 4   3 folds: 8
```

**What the symbols mean**
- layer means one thickness of paper sitting under the punch.
- f means the number of folds made before punching.
- dot situation means choosing the option whose dot lies in the same set of shapes as the one asked.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Holes on unfolding = 2^{f}, where f is the number of folds, provided the punch misses the crease lines. For a pattern or number matrix, find one rule that fits every complete row (a sum, difference, product or a movement) and apply it to the blank. For a dot question, the answer is the figure with a region inside the same shapes. For a hidden figure, trace the target outline inside the design without drawing any new lines.

**Exam-level example**
A sheet folded three times in half and then punched once gives how many holes? The layers double each fold, so 2^{3} = 8 layers and therefore 8 holes. Check the slow way by counting the folds: 1 then 2 then 4 then 8. A classic hidden-figure fact: the five straight lines of a five-pointed star cross to enclose a regular pentagon at the centre, so pentagon is the shape hidden inside a pentagram.

**Common traps**
- Treating folds as adding (2 × 3 = 6) instead of doubling (2^{3} = 8).
- Reading a matrix rule off one row only, before checking it holds on the others.
- In a dot problem, matching the outer shape instead of the dot's region.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| holes = 2^{f} | one hole per layer, and layers double each fold |
| check every row | a matrix rule must fit all complete rows |
| trace, do not add | find a hidden shape without new lines |
keyPoints: Paper folding: holes on unfolding = 2^{f}, where f is the number of folds, if the punch is off the fold lines.
The punched holes appear as mirror images across each fold crease.
Dot situation: pick the figure whose region sits inside the same shapes as the one asked.
Pattern matrix: confirm one rule on every complete row before using it on the blank.
Hidden figure: a pentagram encloses a regular pentagon; trace the outline without adding lines.

items.title: Counting figures — triangles, squares and rectangles
items.body:
### Counting figures — triangles, squares and rectangles

**The idea in one sentence**
Count shapes by first counting the smallest pieces, then the larger shapes they combine into, using simple how-many-ways-to-choose-lines counts so you never miss one or count it twice.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Count the squares in a small 2-by-2 grid by hand. The single cells number 4; the one big 2-by-2 square adds 1; total 5. Now a 3-by-3 grid: single cells number 9; for 2-by-2 squares, slide a two-wide window — it fits in 2 places across and 2 down, giving 4; the full 3-by-3 square adds 1; total 9 + 4 + 1 = 14. You used no formula, only sorted the squares by size and added.

**Why count by size?**
Shapes of different sizes never share the same count, so grouping by size turns one messy figure into a few easy piles you can add safely.

```
 3x3 grid: 1x1 -> 9,  2x2 -> 4,  3x3 -> 1,  total 14
```

**What the symbols mean**
- C(k, 2) means the number of ways to pick 2 things from k, which equals k × (k − 1) ÷ 2.
- apex means the single top point from which the lines are drawn.
- k means how many base points those lines reach.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Triangles from one apex to k base points = C(k, 2) = k × (k − 1) ÷ 2. Squares in an n-by-n grid = 1² + 2² + … + n². Rectangles in an m-by-n cell grid = C(m + 1, 2) × C(n + 1, 2), because every rectangle needs 2 of the horizontal lines and 2 of the vertical lines.

**Exam-level example**
A grid of 2 rows and 3 columns — how many rectangles of all sizes? It has 3 horizontal lines and 4 vertical lines. Choose 2 horizontals: C(3, 2) = 3. Choose 2 verticals: C(4, 2) = 6. Rectangles = 3 × 6 = 18. Check the apex rule the slow way: an apex joined to 4 base points gives C(4, 2) = 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 triangles, which you can even list as ABC, ABD, ABE, ACD, ACE, ADE.

**Common traps**
- Counting only the unit cells and forgetting the larger squares.
- Confusing squares with rectangles; every square is a rectangle, so rectangles are always more.
- Using C(4, 2) when there are five base points; match k to the real number of points.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| C(k, 2) | triangles from an apex to k base points |
| 1² + 2² + … + n² | all squares in an n-by-n grid |
| C(m + 1, 2) × C(n + 1, 2) | all rectangles in an m-by-n grid |
keyPoints: Triangles from one apex to k base points = C(k, 2) = k × (k − 1) ÷ 2 (4 points give 6 triangles).
Squares in an n-by-n grid = 1² + 2² + … + n².
Rectangles in an m-by-n cell grid = C(m + 1, 2) × C(n + 1, 2); a 3-by-3 grid has 14 squares and 36 rectangles.
Every square is also a rectangle, so the square count never exceeds the rectangle count.
Count composite figures by size, smallest first, so none is missed or double-counted.
items.source: local APPSC Group-1 PDF — Non-Verbal Reasoning: Counting Figures (Quadrilateral)

items.title: Figure series, analogy, classification and set overlap
items.body:
### Figure series, analogy, classification and set overlap

**The idea in one sentence**
Most figure puzzles ask you to spot ONE change and then continue it, copy it, or find the figure that breaks it, while overlap questions ask how small or large a shared part can be.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Watch a dot move around the four corners of a square, one corner clockwise at each step. Figure 1 top-left; step clockwise to top-right (Figure 2); again to bottom-right (Figure 3); again to bottom-left (Figure 4). You found Figure 4 just by applying the single move four times, with no trick. The same habit works for a rotating arrow: North, then a quarter-turn clockwise to East, then to South, so three figures land on South.

**Why look for only one change?**
A well-set series applies a single, consistent transformation; inventing a second change is the commonest way people pick the wrong option.

```
 dot: TL -> TR -> BR -> BL   (clockwise, repeats every 4 steps)
```

**What the symbols mean**
- analogy A : B :: C : ? means A becomes B in some way, so do the same thing to C.
- overlap means the part common to two groups.
- minimum and maximum mean the smallest and largest the overlap can be.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Series: extend the one transformation (rotate, move, add or remove, grow). Analogy: apply the exact A-to-B change to C; it may act on the shape (a square loses one side to become a triangle) or on a count (2 dots become 4, a doubling). Classification: keep the property most figures share and drop the exception. Two-group overlap: maximum = the smaller group; minimum = group A + group B − 100% when the two add to more than 100%.

**Exam-level example**
In a town 70% like tea and 80% like coffee; what is the least percentage who like both? Together they total 150%, which overflows 100% by 50%, so at least 50% must like both: minimum = 70 + 80 − 100 = 50%. The most who could like both is capped by the smaller group, 70%. Check the slow way: if only 50% liked both, then tea-only is 20% and coffee-only is 30%, filling exactly 20 + 30 + 50 = 100% with nobody spare, so any smaller overlap would need more than the whole town.

**Common traps**
- Applying two changes in a series that uses only one rule.
- In classification, fixing on the shape when the real odd feature is a dot's position or a count.
- Swapping the minimum overlap (A + B − 100) with the maximum (the smaller group).

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| one change, extended | gives the next figure in a series |
| same change on C | gives the analogy answer |
| maximum = smaller group | the most two groups can share |
| minimum = A + B − 100% | the least they must share |
keyPoints: Figure series: find the single constant change (rotation, movement, add or remove) and extend it.
Figure analogy: apply the exact A-to-B change to C; it may act on the shape or on a count.
Figure classification: keep the property most figures share; the odd one breaks it, often by position or count, not shape.
Maximum overlap of two groups = the smaller group; minimum = A + B − 100% when they add past 100%.
For 70% and 80%: the minimum overlap is 50% and the maximum is 70%.
